security_leads.description: Step 1: Attacker on-path observes the AAF in use and the address pool limitations. Step 2: Attacker impersonates multiple legitimate nodes by spoofing their source addresses in NS(GAAO) requests. Step 3: The 6LR processes each request without validating the identity of the requesting node, assigning addresses/prefixes and depleting the available pool. Step 4: Legitimate nodes are unable to obtain addresses, leading to denial of service.

rfc_references.quote: A rouge node may leverage on this knowledge to carry out address exhaustion attacks by impersonating different nodes and performing multiple requests.

prerequisites: attacker knows the AAF in use
security_leads.mitigation: Implement per-node rate limiting on address requests, use cryptographic identity validation (e.g., CGA or SEND), and enforce strict source address validation at the link layer.

security_leads.description: Step 1: Attacker on-path observes GAAO requests and responses. Step 2: Attacker impersonates multiple legitimate nodes by spoofing source addresses and sending multiple NS(GAAO) requests with different identities. Step 3: The 6LR/6LBR allocates addresses/prefixes for each request, exhausting the available address pool. Step 4: Legitimate nodes are denied address assignments.

rfc_references.quote: A rouge node may leverage on this knowledge to carry out address exhaustion attacks by impersonating different nodes and performing multiple requests.

security_leads.mitigation: Implement link-layer security (e.g., IEEE 802.15.4 security) to prevent spoofing. Enforce per-node address limits and short lifetimes as per RFC8505 Section 7. Use AAFs that provide cryptographic address ownership verification.

security_leads.description: Step 1: Attacker impersonates multiple legitimate nodes by spoofing their source addresses. Step 2: Attacker sends multiple NS(GAAO) requests with different source addresses to the 6LR. Step 3: The 6LR assigns addresses/prefixes to each request, exhausting the available address pool. Step 4: Legitimate nodes are unable to obtain addresses, resulting in denial of service.

rfc_references.quote: A rouge node may leverage on this knowledge to carry out address exhaustion attacks by impersonating different nodes and performing multiple requests.

security_leads.mitigation: Implement link-layer security (e.g., IEEE 802.15.4 security) to prevent spoofing. Enforce per-node address limits and short lifetimes as recommended in RFC8505 Section 7.

security_leads.technique_name: AAF Not Used Error Handling Ambiguity
security_leads.description: Step 1: The specification defines a new error status 'AAF Not Used' (value 13) when a requested AAF is not in use. Step 2: The error handling (Section 5.4) provides three possible actions: re-issue without AAF, re-issue with different AAF, or do nothing. Step 3: The choice is left to configuration, but no guidance is given on how to prevent repeated requests that may consume bandwidth and energy. Step 4: An attacker could force a node to repeatedly retry with different AAFs, causing resource exhaustion or denial of service.

rfc_references.quote: When the node receives this status back it SHOULD perform one of the following actions: ... Re-issue the same request with a different AAF. ... Note that such an approach may lead to repeated requests that may consume bandwidth and energy.

prerequisites: attacker can spoof NA(GAAO) with AAF Not Used status
security_leads.mitigation: Implement rate limiting on retries, enforce a maximum number of retries, or require explicit configuration to limit retry behavior.

security_leads.description: Step 1: Attacker sends NS(GAAO) with an invalid or unsupported AAF value. Step 2: 6LR/6LBR responds with 'AAF Not Used' status. Step 3: Attacker repeatedly re-issues requests with different AAF values, causing multiple NS/NA exchanges. Step 4: This consumes bandwidth and processing resources on the 6LR/6LBR, potentially leading to denial of service.

rfc_references.quote: Re-issue the same request with a different AAF. ... such an approach may lead to repeated requests that may consume bandwidth and energy.

security_leads.mitigation: Rate-limit GAAO requests per source. Configure a maximum number of retries. Use link-layer authentication to filter malicious nodes.

security_leads.description: Step 1: Section 5.3.2 allows GAAO to be piggybacked in RS/RA messages. Step 2: The specification states that a 6LR/6LBR that does not support GAAO will simply ignore the option, and the RA will not include GAAO. Step 3: However, there is no mechanism for the 6LN to distinguish between a 6LR that does not support GAAO and a 6LR that maliciously omits the GAAO. Step 4: An attacker could suppress the GAAO in RA, causing the 6LN to believe GAAO is unsupported and fall back to other mechanisms, potentially leading to address assignment from an untrusted source.

rfc_references.quote: A 6LR/6LBR that does not support GAAO will simply ignore this option, and the corresponding RA message will not include a GAAO. This behavior implicitly signals that the feature is not supported.

prerequisites: attacker can intercept and modify RS/RA messages
security_leads.mitigation: Use secure neighbor discovery (SEND) or link-layer security to protect RS/RA messages; require explicit signaling of GAAO support via the M-flag in 6CIO.

security_leads.description: Step 1: Section 4 defines the R-flag in GAAO. When set in NA(GAAO), the 6LN MUST explicitly register the address/prefix. Step 2: Section 5.2 states that if no registration is received within RETRANS_TIMER * MAX_UNICAST_SOLICIT, the 6LR considers the address/prefix not in use. Step 3: However, the specification does not specify how the 6LR should handle the address/prefix during this waiting period (e.g., whether it is reserved or available to others). Step 4: An attacker could request an address, receive an NA with R-flag set, and then not register, causing the address to be tied up until timeout, enabling a denial-of-service attack on address availability.

rfc_references.quote: When the 6LR/6LBR sets the R-flag in a NA(GAAO) message, it indicates that no registration state has been created and that the requester MUST explicitly register the received address/prefix...

When setting the R-flag, and as for [RFC4861], the 6LR is expect to receive a registration within RETRANS_TIMER multiplied by MAX_UNICAST_SOLICIT. If no registration is received within this amount of time the 6LR will consider that address/prefix is not in use by the requesting 6LN.

prerequisites: attacker can send NS(GAAO) and receive NA(GAAO) with R-flag set
security_leads.mitigation: Implement a short reservation timeout for addresses offered with R-flag set, or require immediate registration to prevent address exhaustion.

security_leads.description: Step 1: Attacker includes a GAAO option in an NS(EARO) or RS message. Step 2: The GAAO option may contain an oversized or malformed Address/Prefix field (128 bits) or ROVR field. Step 3: The 6LR/6LBR processes the option, potentially causing buffer overflow or excessive memory allocation. Step 4: Repeated piggybacked requests can exhaust memory or CPU on constrained devices.

rfc_references.quote: GAAO MAY be used together with the EARO option during address registration phase.
The GAAO MAY be included in the initial RS message

prerequisites: attacker can send NS or RS messages
security_leads.mitigation: Validate GAAO option length against expected size. Implement input sanitization and bounds checking. Use rate limiting for incoming ND messages.
